prompt: In a Python `asyncio` program, one coroutine runs a CPU-heavy loop for 2 seconds without any `await`. What happens to the other coroutines in the same event loop during those 2 seconds?

options.text: The OS preempts the coroutine every few milliseconds so the others keep running
options.explanation: The OS preempts the thread, not individual asyncio tasks. The event loop resumes other coroutines only when control returns to it; an await that completes immediately need not suspend.

options.text: asyncio automatically moves the loop to a background thread
options.explanation: asyncio does nothing of the sort. Offloading needs an explicit `run_in_executor` or `asyncio.to_thread`.

options.text: They keep running in parallel on other cores
options.explanation: An event loop runs on one thread, so its coroutines are never in parallel with each other.

options.text: They all stall until the loop finishes, because the event loop schedules cooperatively
options.explanation: Correct. This CPU loop neither returns nor suspends, so the event loop cannot resume its other tasks. An await only yields if it actually suspends; returning also gives control back.

workedExample: The CPU loop does not return control to the event loop, so other coroutines in that loop stall. The OS may schedule other threads, but resuming this thread continues the same loop. Offload suitable work or yield explicitly with asyncio.sleep(0). In a GIL-enabled interpreter, to_thread can improve responsiveness but does not itself provide parallel execution of pure-Python CPU work; a process pool can.
